summary: Organisational psychologist Adam Grant, a 42-year-old father of three, argues that parents often push children toward careers based on outdated models of success, and that potential is developed rather than innate. He says arts degrees are not useless, soft skills are increasingly valued, and no one can predict what a stable career will look like, especially with generative AI. He draws on his own failures in diving and writing, and says extrinsic rewards are poor measures of mattering.
one_line: Adam Grant says parents should not impose outdated career models on kids, since potential is developed through progress, mentors and soft skills, not innate talent.
key_facts: Adam Grant is a 42-year-old father of three who gives advice to parents on helping kids reach their potential.
Before the global financial crisis, parents told children a finance degree and banking job meant a stable, lucrative career; Grant says those positions then disappeared.
A 2019 study suggested parents pushed children toward STEM degrees because they believed those careers would pay well.
STEM graduates earn more initially, but history, English and social science graduates ultimately catch up, often surpassing their STEM contemporaries.
The term 'soft skills' originated in the 1960s from US Army psychologists developing proficiency in soldiers beyond the 'hard skills' of working with weapons and machines.
A 'very influential person in tech' told Grant it was impossible to plan a career more than a couple of years ahead; when he graduated, Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk hadn't yet finished school.
Grant says directing kids down a path not of their choosing may lead them to fail to thrive or burn out, resent their parents, or rebel and do the opposite.
Grant eventually became a diver on the junior Olympic team, though his school diving coach said he walked like Frankenstein, couldn't touch his toes, and could be outjumped by his grandmother.
Grant has become a New York Times bestselling author three times, but failed the mandatory writing test in his first year at Harvard and had to take a remedial writing course.
Grant says progress can lead to passion just as passion leads to progress, so people should say 'I'm not good at this yet' rather than 'it's not for me'.
In both writing and diving, Grant focused on his own growth and relied on credible mentors, including his diving coach and teachers who believed in him.
Grant argues titles, money and awards are status symbols and 'really poor proxies for mattering'.
